propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of the RAD decision dated March 28, 2019, confirming the RPD decision that applicants are not Convention refugees.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of a decision by the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] dated March 28, 2019, confirming the Refugee Protection Division’s [RPD] decision that the applicants are not Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection, under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [Act].

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of the RAD decision confirming the RPD decision that applicants are not Convention refugees.

propositions.text: Principal applicant Mohammad Ali is a Pakistani citizen who lived mostly in Kuwait and is a successful businessperson; family moved to Lahore in 2012.
propositions.quote: The principal applicant, Mohammad Ali, is a citizen of Pakistan. However, he lived the majority of his life in Kuwait. He is also a successful businessperson. His wife and his two children are citizens of Pakistan as well [collectively, the applicants]. In 2012, they moved from Kuwait to Lahore, Pakistan.

propositions.text: In 2015, the principal applicant received extortion threats and was held at gunpoint; family fled to Canada in 2016 and submitted refugee claim.
propositions.quote: On December 15, 2015, he received an anonymous phone call, demanding money and threatening his life. He sought the help of the police, but without avail. They could only look for the extortionists if they had more details about their identity. On December 25, 2015, masked individuals entered the applicants’ home and held the family at gunpoint, again demanding money. They took jewelry and left on the condition that the principal applicant would pay the rest of the sum demanded, or else his children would be taken. The applicants hid in Khanewal, a village 85 kilometers from Lahore. The principal applicant returned to Lahore on occasion to maintain his small business. The family fled to Canada in February 2016 and submitted a refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the principal applicant's background, extortion threats in Pakistan, and the family's flight to Canada with a refugee claim.

propositions.text: RPD concluded claim was about extortion and general criminality, no nexus to Convention ground, and applicants have an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) to Karachi.
propositions.quote: In a nutshell, the RPD concluded that the applicants’ claim fell under section 97 of the Act – since it was fundamentally about extortion and general criminality, and had no nexus to a Convention ground under section 96. Moreover, the applicants have an Internal Flight Alternative [IFA] to Karachi.

propositions.text: Applicants appealed to RAD arguing RPD erred on nexus and IFA findings.
propositions.quote: The applicants’ appeal to the RAD was two-fold: the RPD erred by finding there was no nexus to a Convention ground and there was a viable IFA in Karachi.

propositions.text: RAD dismissed the appeal, leading to this judicial review application.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismissed the appeal, leading to the present judicial review application.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no nexus to Convention grounds and an IFA to Karachi; applicants appealed to RAD which dismissed appeal; judicial review follows.

propositions.text: Availability of IFA was determinative; court will review RAD's IFA conclusion on reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: The availability of an IFA was determinative of the applicants’ appeal, and it is not necessary today to examine that part of the RAD’s decision dealing with the nexus issue. The RAD’s conclusion with respect to the availability of an IFA to Karachi is reviewable on a reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Court will intervene only if decision lacks justification, transparency, intelligibility, or is outside acceptable range (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick).
propositions.quote: Thus, this Court will only intervene if the decision lacks justification, transparency or intelligibility within the decision‑making process, or that it does not fall within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47).

paragraphs.summary: The court states IFA availability is determinative and will review RAD's IFA conclusion for reasonableness under Dunsmuir standard.

propositions.text: Two-prong test for IFA: no serious persecution risk in area, and it is not unreasonable to seek refuge there (Rasaratnam and Thirunavukkarasu).
propositions.quote: The two-prong test for determining an IFA has been set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in Rasaratnam v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1992] 1 FC 706 (CA) and Thirunavukkarasu v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] 1 FC 589 (CA): (a) First, the Board must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country where it finds an IFA exists; (b) Second, a proposed IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimants, to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites the two-prong Federal Court of Appeal test for IFA: no serious persecution risk and it is reasonable to seek refuge there.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD wrongly said they lived safely in Khanewal though they were hiding; principal applicant only met clients with security in Lahore.
propositions.quote: Before this Court, the applicants submit, however, that the RAD incorrectly characterized the facts where it suggests that they were able to live safely in Khanewal, since they were in hiding. Further, when the principal applicant travelled back to Lahore he only met clients at their places with security and he never returned to his office.

propositions.text: Applicants say ability to hide in Khanewal or Lahore doesn't mean no future risk in Karachi from other criminals.
propositions.quote: The applicants argue that their ability to hide without being located in Khanewal or Lahore should not be taken to mean that they would not be targeted in the future in Karachi by other criminals.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD's conclusion on risk profile is flawed since principal applicant was already extortion victim and perceived as wealthy foreigner.
propositions.quote: The applicants argue that the RAD’s conclusion that the principal applicant does not have a risk profile putting him and his family at risk is flawed since the principal applicant was already the victim of extortion. Indeed, the RAD should have focussed on the applicants’ identities, as perceived wealthy foreigners coming back from Kuwait.

propositions.text: Applicants cite country conditions showing local businesspeople vulnerable to extortion or kidnapping in Karachi.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the applicants further cite country condition documentation showing that local businesspeople are vulnerable to extortion or kidnapping in Karachi.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD wrongly characterized safety in Khanewal, risk in Karachi remains, and RAD ignored their risk profile and country conditions evidence.

propositions.text: Respondent argues applicants did not credibly establish future risk in Pakistan; no evidence linking persecutors to police or politicians.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that the applicants did not credibly establish that they would be at risk of future harm in Pakistan. The applicants could not provide evidence connecting their agents of persecution to the police or local politicians,

propositions.text: Respondent says RAD reasonably concluded problems were local to Lahore and principal applicant lacks risk profile for Karachi targeting.
propositions.quote: and the applicants’ claim that they were targeted because they recently came from Kuwait was rejected by the RAD. The respondent asserts that the RAD reasonably considered documentary evidence and the applicants’ evidence to conclude that their problems were local to Lahore and that the principal applicant did not have a risk profile that would lead him to be targeted in Karachi.

propositions.text: Respondent says applicants' arguments about Karachi unsuitability were speculative and not objectively founded.
propositions.quote: The applicants’ arguments before the RAD about why Karachi was unsuitable were not clear and convincing because their arguments relied on speculation and were not objectively founded.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues applicants failed to prove future risk, RAD reasonably found problems local to Lahore, and applicants' Karachi arguments were speculative.

propositions.text: RAD's conclusion that applicants have viable IFA in Karachi is defensible on facts and law, though another decision-maker might differ.
propositions.quote: While another decision-maker may have decided otherwise, the RAD’s conclusion that the applicants have a viable IFA in Karachi is one that is defensible in respect of the facts and the law.

propositions.text: Impugned decision must be read as a whole.
propositions.quote: The impugned decision must be read as a whole.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD's IFA conclusion defensible and states the decision must be read as a whole.

propositions.text: RAD's suggestion Khanewal was safe does not make decision unreasonable; Khanewal was not identified as IFA, Karachi is large city.
propositions.quote: The mere fact that the RAD suggests that Khanewal was a “safe place” – while in reality the applicants were hiding – do not render the decision unreasonable. Khanewal is only a small village. It was never identified as an IFA. On the other hand, Karachi is a large city with a population between 20 to 24 million people.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD's mention of Khanewal as safe does not make decision unreasonable; Karachi is a large city and not Khanewal was IFA.

propositions.text: Applicants did not credibly show persecutors in Lahore have geographic reach or can trace their movements in Pakistan.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, it is not seriously challenged by the applicants that there is not sufficient credible evidence on record to establish that the agents of persecution in Lahore have geographic reach or capability to learn of the applicants’ return to Pakistan or trace their movements in Pakistan.

propositions.text: Applicants argued police would not assist and they could not identify persecutors.
propositions.quote: The applicants argued that they tried to identify the agents of persecution to no avail and that the police would not assist them;

propositions.text: RAD reasoned police would assist if given more info; no persuasive evidence police or politicians involved in extortion.
propositions.quote: but, the RAD reasoned that the police stated that they would assist the applicants, should they provide additional information about the identity of the extortionists. Further, the applicants did not persuasively demonstrate that the police or politicians were involved in their extortion.

propositions.text: Applicants argued another mafia would locate them as perceived new arrivals from Kuwait.
propositions.quote: The applicants also argued that another “mafia” would locate them wherever they went since they would be perceived as “new” arrivals, notably from Kuwait.

propositions.text: RAD disagreed, noting extortion occurred three years after arrival, so new arrival argument made little sense.
propositions.quote: The RAD disagreed, noting that the applicants were extorted three years after travelling to Lahore and so the principal applicant’s argument that he was extorted because he was a newly arrived businessman from Kuwait was not, in fact, supported by the evidence and “made little sense”.

propositions.text: Applicants could not provide credible evidence that persecutors tried to locate them at brother-in-law’s house or further threats after leaving Pakistan.
propositions.quote: Further, the applicants could not provide to the RPD or the RAD any credible evidence to show that the agents of persecution tried to locate them at the principal applicant’s brother-in-law’s house either, and did not have follow-up information regarding whether there were further threats directed at their family since they left Pakistan.

propositions.text: No reviewable error found in these factual conclusions or inferences.
propositions.quote: I fail to see any reviewable error in these conclusions or inferences of fact.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no credible evidence that persecutors have geographic reach or that police or politicians were involved; no reviewable error in RAD's findings.

propositions.text: Applicants complain RAD failed to examine relevant documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The applicants also complain that the RAD failed to examine relevant documentary evidence.

propositions.text: Court disagrees; RAD cited country condition documents showing internal relocation possible, especially in large cities like Karachi.
propositions.quote: I kindly disagree. The RAD cited country condition documentation to show that internal relocation is possible in Pakistan, notably in large urban centres.

propositions.text: RAD found kidnapping and extortion risks apply to high profile politicians, not principal applicant, and children kidnapping not linked to extortion or small businesspeople.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that documentary evidence showed that kidnapping and extortion are risks for high profile politicians or members of government, unlike the principal applicant. And, although there is evidence that children are at risk of kidnapping, it is not associated with extortion and small businesspeople.

propositions.text: This conclusion is reasonable.
propositions.quote: This conclusion is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants say RAD ignored evidence; court finds RAD reasonably considered country conditions showing internal relocation possible and risks limited to high profile persons.

propositions.text: Applicants rely on DOS report stating criminals target businessmen and prominent families for ransom.
propositions.quote: Indeed, where one has a closer look to the United States Department of State [DOS] Report upon which the applicants rely, the statement that “[c]riminal and extremist groups often target local businessmen and prominent families to extort ransoms for profit or to finance operations” is not in contradiction with the RAD’s finding that the principal applicant’s profile “does not rise to a level of wealth and prominence as described as being at risk in the documentary evidence”.

propositions.text: Court finds DOS report statement not contradictory to RAD's finding that principal applicant's profile is not at risk level described in evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD is entitled to deference for its weighing of the evidence and its reasoning is intelligible. This Court should not reweigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants cite DOS report on targeting businessmen; court finds this does not contradict RAD's finding on principal applicant's risk profile and defers to RAD.

propositions.text: RAD concluded no persuasive evidence Karachi would be unreasonable IFA; police registration not centralized and applicants not sought by police.
propositions.quote: Finally, the RAD concluded that there was no persuasive evidence to suggest that Karachi would be an unreasonable IFA. Although the applicants will have to register with the police as tenants in Karachi, the police do not have a centralized database and so the information will not be available in other regions; and, the applicants are not being sought by the police.

propositions.text: Applicants would not suffer undue hardship relocating to Karachi; they are well educated and have previously lived abroad without problems.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the applicants would not suffer undue hardship relocating to Karachi. Indeed, both the principal applicant and his wife are well educated by Pakistani standards. Further, while it is true that they do not have family support outside Lahore, they previously lived in Kuwait and later travelled to Canada; they have not reported any problems due to lack of family support.

propositions.text: No reviewable error found in these conclusions or inferences of fact.
propositions.quote: Again, I fail to see any reviewable error in these conclusions or inferences of fact.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably concluded Karachi is a reasonable IFA and applicants would not face undue hardship relocating there.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed; no question of general importance certified.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application and does not certify any question of general importance.
